uncited: Composite Depth Cueing and Directional Shading is a frequency-domain rendering technique that simultaneously applies linear depth cueing (attenuation) and hemispherical directional shading to volume data.
It solves the problem of efficiently computing both effects within the Fourier Projection-Slice framework, where naive spatial-domain computation would be prohibitively expensive.

It sets itself apart from its parent method, [Linear Depth Cueing via Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem](1129-linear-depth-cueing-via-fourier-projection-slice-theorem.md), by combining the attenuation model with a hemispherical illumination model that avoids the nonlinear absolute value operator, allowing the lighting direction to be factored out of the integral.
*   **Input:** Volume of albedo $\Omega(x,y,z)$, orientation field $N(x,y,z)$, depth vector field $D(x,y,z)$, viewing direction $V$, and lighting direction $L$.
The method relies on 16 precomputed 3D spectra.
These are derived from the albedo volume $\Omega$ and the geometric fields $N$ and $D$.
*   **VL Vector:** A 12-element vector of products of viewing direction components $V$ and lighting direction components $L$.
*   Layout: $(V_x L_x, V_x L_y, V_x L_z, V_y L_x, V_y L_y, V_y L_z, V_z L_x, V_z L_y, V_z L_z, V_x, V_y, V_z, L_x, L_y, L_z)$.
*   *Note: The source lists 13 elements in the tuple but refers to it as a 12-element vector in the text.
The standard expansion of $(V \cdot L)$ terms plus linear terms usually yields specific counts.
*   **DN Vector:** A 12-element vector of products of depth vector components $D$ and orientation components $N$.
*   Layout: $(D_x N_x, D_x N_y, D_x N_z, D_y N_x, D_y N_y, D_y N_z, D_z N_x, D_z N_y, D_z N_z, D_x, D_y, D_z, N_x, N_y, N_z)$.
*   *Note: Similar to VL, the tuple has 13 elements.
*   $VL \cdot \Pi_V [\dots]$ denotes the dot product between the $VL$ vector and the corresponding vector of projected spectra.
Create four copies of the weighted albedo volume: $I_s \Omega(x,y,z)$, $I_s \Omega(x,y,z) N_x(x,y,z)$, $I_s \Omega(x,y,z) N_y(x,y,z)$, and $I_s \Omega(x,y,z) N_z(x,y,z)$.
Create four copies of the weighted albedo volume scaled by depth components: $I_s \Omega(x,y,z) D_x(x,y,z)$, $I_s \Omega(x,y,z) D_y(x,y,z)$, $I_s \Omega(x,y,z) D_z(x,y,z)$, and $I_s \Omega(x,y,z)$.
The derivation involves expanding the product of the hemispherical term $(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} N \cdot L)$ and the depth cueing term $(\frac{\tau}{2} + \frac{\tau}{2} D \cdot V)$.
The expansion results in terms involving $1, N_i, D_j, N_i D_j$.
The specific 16 spectra correspond to the basis functions needed to reconstruct the dot products in the VL and DN vectors.
Specifically, one needs spectra for $\Omega$, $\Omega N_i$, $\Omega D_j$, and $\Omega N_i D_j$.*
Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of each of the 16 basis volumes to yield the 16 precomputed spectra.
Extract 2D slices from each of the 16 precomputed 3D spectra along the direction $V$.
Compute the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform of each extracted slice to obtain spatial domain images.
Weight each image by the corresponding coefficient from the $VL$ and $DN$ vectors and the constant $c_3$.
*   The term $\Pi_V [(1/2 + 1/2 DN) I_s \Omega]$ is computed by combining the projected spectra weighted by the $DN$ components.
*   The term $\Pi_V [I_s \Omega]$ is the projection of the base albedo.

Where $\text{Image}_k$ are the inverse-transformed slices corresponding to the basis functions in the $DN$ vector, and $\text{Image}_{\text{base}}$ is the inverse-transformed slice of the base albedo spectrum.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Requires storing 16 3D spectra.
*   **When to Use:** Large volumes where asymptotic efficiency outweighs constant overhead; scenes requiring both depth cueing and directional shading.
*   **When Not to Use:** Small volumes; hardware with limited memory; scenes requiring accurate ambient lighting or emission.
The method was developed by Marc Levoy as part of his work on Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering.
The technique was demonstrated on a CT scan of a human skull.
The approach was implemented in C on a Silicon Graphics 4D/320 VGX.
